lesson.title: One More Unit: An Introduction to Marginal Analysis
lesson.summary: In economics the derivative of a total function is called its marginal function, and it estimates the effect of exactly one more unit, the differential approximation with dx fixed at 1.
lesson.body:
Every differential approximation so far has treated dx as any small step you like. Economics tends to care about one particular step size above all others: one more unit, one more item produced, one more hour worked. Set dx = 1 in the differential approximation f(a + dx) is approximately f(a) + f'(a) dx, and the predicted change collapses to just f'(a). That single number, the derivative evaluated at the current quantity, is what economists call the marginal value of the function at that point. It rests directly on the derivative function and instantaneous rate ideas: f'(x) is a rate of change built as a limit, and marginal analysis simply asks what that rate predicts for the very next unit.

This is a vocabulary point worth getting right immediately. In everyday English, "marginal" often means small or unimportant. In economics, marginal means exactly one thing: the derivative, the rate at which a total quantity changes per additional unit. A "marginal" effect is not necessarily small; it is simply the effect of one more unit, and it can be large.

Here is the idea with real numbers. Suppose a factory's total cost to produce x items is C(x) = 0.01x^2 + 5x + 100 dollars. The marginal cost function is C'(x) = 0.02x + 5. At x = 100 units already produced, C'(100) = 0.02(100) + 5 = 2 + 5 = 7 dollars, meaning the 101st item is predicted to cost about $7 to make. Checking directly: C(100) = 0.01(10000) + 500 + 100 = 700 dollars, and C(101) = 0.01(10201) + 505 + 100 = 707.01 dollars, so the actual cost of that 101st item was 707.01 - 700 = 7.01 dollars, matching the marginal estimate to within a penny.

The next three chapters apply this same idea to the three quantities businesses track most closely: cost, revenue, and profit. Marginal analysis is the general principle; marginal cost, marginal revenue, and marginal profit are its most common applications.
